claims.text: The equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni quinary alloy is single-phase FCC after the specified thermomechanical processing.
The equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets are single-phase FCC after the specified thermomechanical processing.
Identical thermomechanical processing can produce comparable grain size and texture across the quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys.
The greater compositional complexity of the quinary alloy produces more pronounced local lattice distortion than in the lower-component alloys.
The greater compositional complexity of the quinary alloy promotes more effective chemical short-range order than in the lower-component alloys.
Enhanced local lattice distortion impedes or pins dislocation motion.
Chemical short-range order impedes or pins dislocation motion and modifies slip behavior.
Stronger dislocation pinning increases yield strength.
Stronger dislocation pinning and modified slip behavior increase strain hardening.
The quaternary alloys will have lower yield strengths than the quinary baseline under identical test conditions.
The ternary alloys will have lower yield strengths than the quinary baseline under identical test conditions.
The quaternary and ternary alloys will have lower strain-hardening rates than the quinary baseline.
The quaternary and ternary alloys will initiate failure earlier than the quinary baseline.
The proposed comparison is applicable only while all alloys remain single-phase FCC and have comparable grain sizes and textures.
The alloys should be compared at the same room temperature and strain rate.
The relative contributions of lattice distortion and chemical short-range order to dislocation behavior are uncertain.
